The next scene after the rampart's eventual leveling shows Gog and Magog surging together, completing its temporary access-control arc.
It explicitly names Gog and Magog breaking open and rushing down every elevation, the decisive later reversal of the focus's blocked ascent and penetration.
Barriers placed before and behind prevent perception and forward access, a close image of comprehensive obstruction.
A wall with a gate divides mercy within from punishment outside, directly depicting a boundary that regulates access and outcome.
The barrier and forbidden partition between the two seas give a direct physical-boundary parallel.

God's placing of a barrier between the two seas supplies another explicit physical-boundary parallel.
The devils cannot penetrate the exalted assembly to listen, closely paralleling denied access across a guarded boundary.
The heavens are found filled with powerful guards and flames, a close celestial image of an inaccessible protected domain.
Former listening stations become guarded by waiting flames, showing a boundary whose attempted penetration is actively denied.
A barrier separates the Garden and the Fire, making access and position consequential across a clear boundary.
The barzakh behind the dead holds until resurrection, a temporal boundary parallel to the focus's temporary rampart.
A hidden barrier prevents disbelievers from receiving the recitation, a metaphorical counterpart to blocked access.
Coverings on hearts and deafness in ears make reception inaccessible, a related metaphor of prevented entry.

The protected roof of heaven supplies a broad cosmic analogue to a constructed protective enclosure.
Heaven is guarded against expelled devils, establishing divine protection through denied approach.
The guarded heaven's protection from every rebellious devil is a close general parallel to the rampart's defensive purpose.
Devils are repelled from the heavenly boundary and punished if they attempt access, extending the guarded-access pattern.
A stolen hearing is pursued by a visible flame, showing attempted penetration of a guarded domain being stopped.
The nearest heaven is guarded against devils by missile-like flames, a further celestial access-control parallel.
Humans and jinn cannot pass beyond the regions of heaven and earth without authority, directly framing an uncrossable limit.
Protective armour is taught to shield people in battle, a material-protection analogue to the rampart's defensive fabrication.
The instruction to make measured coats of mail provides a close metalworking and protective-use counterpart to the rampart's construction.
God provides shelters and protective garments, supplying the broader theology of divinely enabled protection.
Those who trusted their fortresses learn that built defenses cannot stand against God's decree, qualifying the focus's temporary mercy.
Fortified towns and walls describe defensive separation, though the passage exposes their limits rather than their success.
Death reaches people even in fortified towers, a consequential contrast to treating any enclosure as absolute protection.
No refuge can protect from God's command except His mercy, directly qualifying the focus's later description of the rampart as mercy.
The challenge to ascend through heavenly means offers a distant ascent-boundary parallel and exposes illegitimate claims to access.
An opened gate in heaven would permit ascent, functioning as a contrast to the focus's denied upward route.
The response to an opened heavenly gate still denies perception, a remote counterpart to access being blocked or ineffective.
Pharaoh's proposed tower to reach heavenly means is a failed human attempt to overcome a higher boundary.
